questions.prompt: An API test gets HTTP 200 but the returned object has the wrong owner. What should the test add?

choices.text: Replace the API assertion with a browser screenshot only.
Treat every response from the expected host as correct.
Assert the relevant response body fields.
Remove payload checks because status proves all behavior.

questions.explanation: Success status and payload correctness are separate. A test should verify the contract fields relevant to the scenario.

sources.title: Playwright API testing
sources.claim: Playwright API testing checks status and response payloads and can prepare server state before browser verification.

questions.prompt: A test calls context.request to log in. Where can response cookies be available?

choices.text: Nowhere, because APIRequestContext discards all cookies.
In the associated browser context.
Only in a new unrelated browser process created later.
In every independent request context across the test suite.

questions.explanation: Browser-associated request contexts share cookie storage. Independent contexts are isolated rather than globally synchronized.

sources.title: Playwright API testing
sources.claim: Browser-associated APIRequestContext shares cookies with its BrowserContext; independently created request contexts have isolated cookies.

questions.prompt: Two tests should start with separate cookies and local storage. Which Playwright boundary supports that?

choices.text: Separate browser contexts.
Separate pages in the same shared context only.
Different locator variable names on one shared page.
One persistent context reused without cleanup by all tests.

questions.explanation: Browser contexts isolate browser state. Pages in the same context can share that state; variable names provide no isolation.

sources.title: Playwright isolation
sources.claim: Playwright uses separate browser contexts for isolated tests, preventing cookies and local storage from leaking between tests.

questions.prompt: A fresh browser context still sees records created by a previous test in the database. Why?

choices.text: Every browser context restores the server database automatically.
Cookies are the only place a server can store records.
Creating a new page always rolls back every prior API request.
Browser isolation does not clear remote server data.

questions.explanation: Browser state and server persistence are different boundaries. Tests need explicit server-state setup and cleanup where required.

sources.title: Playwright API testing
sources.claim: API tests can create resources for browser scenarios and remove them during teardown; browser isolation alone does not reset remote application data.

questions.prompt: A create endpoint should return the submitted title. Which assertion complements the success status?

choices.text: Assert that every API response has the same byte length.
Accept any body whenever the status is below 400.
Check the returned resource title against the submitted value.
Check only that the request object existed before sending.

questions.explanation: A relevant payload assertion checks the intended contract. Object existence, response length and broad status ranges do not verify the title.

sources.title: Playwright API testing
sources.claim: API status and returned resource data are separate contract checks.

questions.prompt: A standalone request context logs in, and a later browser context needs that state. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Expect cookies to transfer solely because both use the same base URL.
Export storage state and initialize the browser context with it.
Assume every browser automatically receives the standalone cookie jar.
Initialize an unrelated browser context without exporting the API cookie state.

questions.explanation: Storage state can be transferred deliberately. Common URLs and variable names do not merge independent context storage.

sources.title: Playwright API testing
sources.claim: Standalone APIRequestContext has isolated cookie storage and can export storage state.

questions.prompt: Which checks belong in a targeted API test? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assert the expected status for the operation.
Verify relevant fields in the response payload.
A successful status replaces the need to validate the response contract fields.
Treat response.ok as proof every returned field is correct.
Skip authorization-related response checks in authenticated flows.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Status is part of the endpoint contract. B is correct: The body can be incorrect despite a successful status. C is incorrect: Status success and body correctness must be checked separately. D is incorrect: Status classification does not validate data. E is incorrect: Authenticated scenarios still need their access outcome verified.

sources.title: Playwright API testing
sources.claim: Playwright API testing checks status and response payloads and can prepare server state before browser verification.

questions.prompt: Which request-context cookie statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Set-Cookie responses can update the associated browser context.
An independently created request context has isolated cookies.
Every request context automatically shares one global cookie store.
A standalone API login always authenticates all open browser contexts.
Browser-associated API requests share browser-context cookies.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Shared storage supports API login before browser steps. B is correct: It does not automatically update another browser context. C is incorrect: Independent contexts are separate. D is incorrect: State must be deliberately shared or exported. E is correct: They use the same cookie jar.

sources.title: Playwright API testing
sources.claim: Browser-associated APIRequestContext shares cookies with its BrowserContext; independently created request contexts have isolated cookies.

questions.prompt: Which isolation statements follow Playwright’s model? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Creating a second page in the same context clears its existing cookies.
Two pages in the same browser context have isolated cookie stores by default.
All pages in one context necessarily have independent cookie jars.
Separate browser contexts can isolate cookies and storage.
Fresh contexts reduce dependence on the order of earlier tests.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: A new page in the same context shares existing context storage. B is incorrect: Pages share their containing context’s cookies and storage. C is incorrect: They share the context’s storage. D is correct: Context boundaries separate browser state. E is correct: A clean starting state prevents state leakage.

sources.title: Playwright isolation
sources.claim: Playwright uses separate browser contexts for isolated tests, preventing cookies and local storage from leaking between tests.

questions.prompt: Which fixture practices fit API-assisted browser tests? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Keep test fixtures scoped so one test does not rely on another’s record.
Treat the same shared mutable record as automatic test isolation.
Create needed records through controlled API setup.
Remove test-created resources during teardown where appropriate.
Assume a new browser context resets the production database.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Independent fixtures reduce order dependence. B is incorrect: Concurrent tests can interfere with shared data. C is correct: Setup establishes the scenario explicitly. D is correct: Cleanup avoids persistent test-data interference. E is incorrect: Context isolation is local browser state.

sources.title: Playwright API testing
sources.claim: API tests can create resources for browser scenarios and remove them during teardown; browser isolation alone does not reset remote application data.
